items.stem: A company is moving an application to Amazon EC2 instances in two Availability Zones. The instances must read and write the same set of files at the same time. The instances run Linux and access the files over NFS. The company wants to move the files from its data center to AWS without changing the application. Which storage solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: The instances run Linux and access the files over NFS

options.text: Create an Amazon EFS file system with a mount target in each Availability Zone, and mount the file system on every instance.
options.why: The Linux instances keep their NFS mounts, because EFS uses [NFS v4](../facts/efs.md#efs-faq-nfs-v4-protocol) and serves instances in several zones [concurrently from multiple NFS clients](../facts/efs.md#efs-concurrent-access-multiple-clients-multiple-azs).

options.text: Create an Amazon FSx for Windows File Server Multi-AZ file system that is joined to Active Directory, and map its share on every instance.
options.why: It serves files over [the SMB protocol](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-faq-windows-smb-protocol) and needs an Active Directory domain, which the Linux NFS clients do not use.
options.misconception: picks the Windows SMB file system for Linux clients that use NFS

options.text: Install file server software on a new EC2 instance with a large Amazon EBS volume, and share the files from it with every instance.
options.why: It can work, but the company runs and patches the file server itself, while EFS is [serverless, fully elastic file storage](../facts/efs.md#efs-serverless-elastic-no-provisioning).

options.text: Create one Amazon EBS io2 volume with Multi-Attach turned on, and attach the volume to every instance in both Availability Zones.
options.why: Multi-Attach attaches one io2 volume to instances [in the same Availability Zone](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-multi-attach-provisioned-iops-same-az), so the instances in the second zone cannot attach it.

items.explanation: Linux clients that share files over NFS fit Amazon EFS. A Regional file system stores data across [multiple geographically separated Availability Zones](../facts/efs.md#efs-regional-recommended-type), and each zone gets a mount target, so both zones read and write the same files. AWS runs the storage, so the company has no file server to patch.
items.takeaway: Linux instances that share files over NFS across zones: Amazon EFS.
items.twin: If the stem said "The instances run Windows Server, and users reach the files through SMB shares with permissions from the company's Active Directory" instead: FSx for Windows File Server, because EFS on Windows instances [is not supported](../facts/efs.md#efs-windows-ec2-not-supported).
items.say: Linux and NFS across zones means EFS: a managed shared file system with a mount target in each zone.

solvers.stem_only: Linux clients, NFS, concurrent shared read/write across two AZs, no app change, least overhead: Amazon EFS (Regional) with a mount target in each AZ, mounted on all instances.

items.stem: A company runs a serverless document-processing application. Many AWS Lambda functions run at the same time, and all of them must read and update the same set of files with standard file operations. The files must persist between invocations and must be visible to every function. The functions already connect to a VPC in one AWS Region. Which storage solution meets these requirements?
keywords: the same set of files with standard file operations

options.text: Write the files to the /tmp directory of each function, and read the files back from /tmp in later invocations.
options.why: /tmp is [temporary and unique to each execution environment](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-tmp-unique-per-environment), so other functions do not see the files, and the files are not guaranteed to persist.

options.text: Create an Amazon EBS gp3 volume, and attach the volume to each function when the function starts to process a request.
options.why: Block storage is [attached to single Amazon EC2 instances or containers](../facts/efs.md#efs-decision-guide-block-row-single-instance), so it is not a file system that many functions share.
options.misconception: believes that a function can attach a block volume as an instance does

options.text: Create an Amazon EFS file system with mount targets in the VPC, and configure each function to mount the file system.
options.why: A function can [mount an Amazon Elastic File System](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-efs-shared-mount-in-vpc) to a local directory and [access and modify shared resources safely](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-efs-shared-mount-in-vpc) at high concurrency.

options.text: Store the files as objects in an Amazon S3 bucket, and read and write the objects with the S3 API from each function.
options.why: S3 is an [object storage service](../facts/efs.md#efs-faq-use-case-file-vs-block-vs-object), so the code uses API calls instead of the standard file operations that the stem requires.
options.misconception: treats object storage as a file system

items.explanation: Many functions need one shared set of files with standard file operations. You can access EFS from Lambda by referencing [an EFS file system in your function settings](../facts/efs.md#efs-faq-access-from-lambda-function-settings), and the function reaches it [over the local network in a VPC](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-efs-shared-mount-in-vpc). The files stay in EFS between invocations.
items.takeaway: Lambda functions that share files and keep them between invocations mount Amazon EFS.
items.twin: If the stem said "each function needs scratch space for one invocation only" instead: the /tmp directory, because /tmp is [temporary and unique to each execution environment](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-tmp-unique-per-environment).

solvers.stem_only: Shared, persistent POSIX file storage for many concurrent VPC-connected Lambda functions: Amazon EFS with mount targets in the VPC (via an access point), configured as the function file system.

items.stem: A company runs a Linux application on Amazon EC2 instances in several Availability Zones. The instances share a data set over NFS. The data set grows by an unpredictable amount each week, and old files are deleted at irregular times. The company wants scalable shared storage. The team must never run out of space and does not want to plan, size or grow the storage capacity. Which storage solution meets these requirements?
keywords: grows by an unpredictable amount each week
does not want to plan, size or grow the storage capacity
share a data set over NFS

options.text: Create an Amazon EFS file system, and add an Amazon CloudWatch alarm and a Lambda function that raise the file system size when it is almost full.
options.why: EFS file systems are [elastic, automatically growing and shrinking](../facts/efs.md#efs-faq-elastic-grow-shrink), so there is no size to raise, and the alarm and function add work.

options.text: Create an Amazon FSx for OpenZFS file system with SSD storage, and set its storage capacity to the size that the team expects next year.
options.why: With SSD storage you specify a size and [pay for the amount of storage](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-openzfs-two-storage-classes-intelligent-tiering-and-ssd) that you provision, so the team still plans capacity.
options.misconception: treats a file system with a set size as elastic storage

options.text: Attach an Amazon EBS gp3 volume to each instance, and increase the size of each volume with Elastic Volumes when the data grows.
options.why: Block storage is [attached to single Amazon EC2 instances or containers](../facts/efs.md#efs-decision-guide-block-row-single-instance), so the instances do not share one data set, and someone grows each volume.
options.misconception: believes that a volume on each instance gives the instances one shared data set

options.text: Create an Amazon EFS file system with a mount target in each Availability Zone, and mount the file system on every instance.
options.why: EFS grows and shrinks [without provisioning or managing storage capacity](../facts/efs.md#efs-serverless-elastic-no-provisioning), and instances in several zones share it over NFS.

items.explanation: The team wants no capacity planning and no resizing work. Amazon EFS is [serverless, fully elastic file storage](../facts/efs.md#efs-serverless-elastic-no-provisioning), and a file system is [elastic, automatically growing and shrinking](../facts/efs.md#efs-faq-elastic-grow-shrink) as files are added and removed. There is no size to set, so the data set can grow without work.
items.takeaway: Shared Linux storage with no size to plan or grow: Amazon EFS.
items.twin: If the stem said "one instance needs a block device for a database" instead: an Amazon EBS volume, because block storage is [attached to single Amazon EC2 instances or containers](../facts/efs.md#efs-decision-guide-block-row-single-instance).

solvers.stem_only: Shared NFS storage across AZs that grows and shrinks automatically with no capacity planning: Amazon EFS (elastic storage), mount target per AZ.

items.stem: A company runs Microsoft SQL Server failover cluster instances on Amazon EC2 instances that run Windows Server in two Availability Zones. The cluster needs shared storage over SMB for the database files. The storage must be highly available across the two Availability Zones and must give the low latency that a database needs. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)
keywords: highly available across the two Availability Zones

options.text: Create an Amazon EFS Regional file system with mount targets in both Availability Zones, and store the database files on the file system.
options.why: The cluster nodes run Windows Server, and using EFS with Windows instances [is not supported](../facts/efs.md#efs-windows-ec2-not-supported).

options.text: Create an Amazon FSx for Windows File Server Multi-AZ file system with SSD storage, and join it to the company's Active Directory domain.
options.why: Multi-AZ uses [a preferred AZ and a standby AZ](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-windows-multi-az-standby-two-azs-sync-replication), and [SSD storage is recommended for SQL Server](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-windows-sql-server-ssd-recommended).

options.text: Create one Amazon EBS io2 volume with Multi-Attach turned on, and attach the volume to the cluster nodes in both Availability Zones.
options.why: Multi-Attach works for instances [in the same Availability Zone](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-multi-attach-provisioned-iops-same-az), so the node in the second zone cannot attach the volume.

options.text: Create continuously available (CA) file shares on the FSx file system, and store the SQL Server data files and log files on those shares.
options.why: For SQL Server, AWS requires that you [use CA shares on Multi-AZ file systems](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-windows-ca-shares-required-multi-az-for-sql-server).

options.text: Build a Windows file server cluster on two more EC2 instances in the two Availability Zones, and share their EBS volumes over SMB.
options.why: It can work, but the team builds, patches and fails over the file servers itself, while FSx gives [fully managed Microsoft Windows file servers](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-windows-fully-managed-native-windows-file-servers-smb).

items.explanation: The cluster needs SMB storage that both zones reach. FSx for Windows File Server can be [storage for active data files](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-windows-sql-server-active-data-files-or-share-witness-ssd) of high availability SQL Server. A Multi-AZ file system keeps the shares available by [failing over automatically to the standby AZ](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-windows-multi-az-enhanced-durability-availability-auto-failover).
items.takeaway: SQL Server clusters across two zones on SMB: FSx for Windows Multi-AZ with SSD and CA shares.
items.twin: If the stem said "one SQL Server instance in one Availability Zone that uses block storage" instead: an Amazon EBS volume, because block storage is [attached to single Amazon EC2 instances or containers](../facts/efs.md#efs-decision-guide-block-row-single-instance).

solvers.stem_only: SQL Server FCI shared SMB storage across two AZs with low latency: Amazon FSx for Windows File Server Multi-AZ with SSD storage joined to AD, and continuously available (CA) shares holding the data and log files.

items.stem: A company stores about 100 GiB of application data on an Amazon EFS Regional file system that uses Bursting throughput. The file system has used all of its burst credits, and the application slows down. The throughput is spiky and unpredictable: the application is idle most of the day, then drives short peaks. The company must restore the performance of the application. Which change will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?

options.text: Switch the file system to Elastic throughput, so that throughput scales up and down with the reads and writes of the application.
options.why: Elastic fits [spiky or unpredictable workloads](../facts/efs.md#efs-elastic-best-for-spiky-low-average-to-peak), and you [pay only for the amount of metadata](../facts/efs.md#efs-elastic-scales-automatically-no-provisioning-pay-per-use) and data that the application reads and writes.

options.text: Switch the file system to Provisioned throughput, and set the provisioned level to the throughput that the application needs at its peak.
options.why: It works, but you are [charged for the amount of throughput enabled](../facts/efs.md#efs-provisioned-billed-for-throughput-enabled) all day, although the application is idle most of the time.

options.text: Keep Bursting throughput, and store extra unused data in the file system to raise the baseline throughput that the file system earns.
options.why: Bursting gives [throughput that scales with the amount of storage](../facts/efs.md#efs-bursting-scales-with-storage-size-recommended-for), so the company pays to store data that nobody reads.

options.text: Create a new file system that uses the Max I/O performance mode, and copy the application data to the new file system.
options.why: Max I/O changes the performance mode, not the throughput mode, and AWS recommends [always using General Purpose performance mode](../facts/efs.md#efs-general-purpose-always-recommended-max-io-higher-latency).

items.explanation: The file system ran out of burst credits, and its load is spiky and unpredictable. Elastic throughput [scales automatically](../facts/efs.md#efs-elastic-scales-automatically-no-provisioning-pay-per-use), so the short peaks get the throughput that they need. The company pays for the reads and writes, not for a level that stays unused through the idle hours.
items.takeaway: Spiky or unpredictable EFS throughput: Elastic throughput, which charges for what the application uses.
items.twin: If the stem said "The application drives a steady-state, predictable throughput close to its peak all day" instead: Provisioned throughput, because it fits [predictable and high levels of sustained throughput requirements](../facts/efs.md#efs-pricing-provisioned-throughput-predictable-sustained).
items.say: Spiky and hard to forecast means Elastic throughput: it scales with the load, and you pay for what you use.

solvers.stem_only: Spiky, unpredictable throughput with burst credits exhausted: switch the EFS file system to Elastic throughput (pay for what is used).

items.stem: A company runs a Linux application on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group. The instances share a set of files through an Amazon EFS file system. The files are development build artifacts that the team can re-create, and a loss of access during an Availability Zone outage is acceptable. The company plans to create a new file system for these files. Which file system configuration will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?
keywords: development build artifacts that the team can re-create
a loss of access during an Availability Zone outage is acceptable

options.text: Create an EFS One Zone file system in one Availability Zone, and keep the automatic backups of the new file system turned on.
options.why: One Zone suits [development, build, and staging environments](../facts/efs.md#efs-faq-one-zone-use-cases), and the stem accepts a loss of access during a zone outage.

options.text: Create an EFS Regional file system that stores data across Availability Zones, and create a mount target in each zone.
options.why: It works, but it pays for availability that the stem does not need, because One Zone fits applications that [do not require the Multi-AZ availability and durability](../facts/efs.md#efs-pricing-one-zone-for-no-multi-az-need).

options.text: Create an EFS Regional file system, and configure EFS Replication to a destination file system in a second AWS Region.
options.why: It works, but it adds a second file system in a [Region or Availability Zone (AZ) of your choice](../facts/efs.md#efs-replication-destination-faq-region-or-az-of-choice) for files that the team can re-create.
options.misconception: adds a second Region for files that the team can re-create

options.text: Create two EFS One Zone file systems in two Availability Zones, and keep them in sync with a scheduled AWS DataSync task.
options.why: Two file systems and a sync task cost more than one One Zone file system, and the stem accepts a loss of access during a zone outage.
options.misconception: keeps two copies in sync instead of choosing the file system type that fits

items.explanation: The team can re-create the files, and the stem accepts a loss of access during a zone outage. One Zone file systems [store data redundantly within a single AZ](../facts/efs.md#efs-faq-one-zone-single-az), and AWS names them for [development, build, and staging environments](../facts/efs.md#efs-faq-one-zone-use-cases). One zone is the cheapest fit. Backups do not decide it; from the CLI they are [enabled by default only for One Zone](../facts/efs.md#efs-backup-cli-api-default-only-one-zone).
items.takeaway: Re-creatable development files and an accepted zone outage: EFS One Zone.
items.twin: If the stem said "The files are production reports, and the file system must be highly available if one Availability Zone fails" instead: a Regional file system, because it gives [continuous availability to the data](../facts/efs.md#efs-regional-multi-az-continuous-availability).

solvers.stem_only: Re-creatable data where loss of access during an AZ outage is acceptable, cheapest: EFS One Zone storage class in one AZ.

The instances run Windows Server, and users reach the files through SMB shares with permissions from the company's Active Directory. The company wants to move the files from its data center to AWS without changing the application. Which storage solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: SMB shares with permissions from the company's Active Directory

options.text: Create an Amazon EFS file system with a mount target in each Availability Zone, and mount the file system on every instance.
options.why: Using EFS with Windows instances [is not supported](../facts/efs.md#efs-windows-ec2-not-supported), so the Windows Server instances cannot use the file system.

options.text: Create an Amazon FSx for Windows File Server Multi-AZ file system that is joined to Active Directory, and map its share on every instance.
options.why: It gives [fully managed Microsoft Windows file servers](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-windows-fully-managed-native-windows-file-servers-smb) over SMB, and you [join it to your Active Directory domain](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-windows-joins-active-directory-for-authentication-and-acls) for the permissions.

options.text: Install file server software on a new EC2 instance with a large Amazon EBS volume, and share the files from it with every instance.
options.why: It can work, but the company runs and patches the Windows file server itself, while FSx gives [fully managed Microsoft Windows file servers](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-windows-fully-managed-native-windows-file-servers-smb).

options.text: Create one Amazon EBS io2 volume with Multi-Attach turned on, and attach the volume to every instance in both Availability Zones.
options.why: Multi-Attach attaches one io2 volume to instances [in the same Availability Zone](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-multi-attach-provisioned-iops-same-az), so the instances in the second zone cannot attach it.

items.explanation: Windows Server instances that use SMB shares with Active Directory permissions fit FSx for Windows File Server. The domain provides [user authentication and file- and folder-level access control](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-windows-joins-active-directory-for-authentication-and-acls), so the shares keep their permissions. AWS manages the file servers, so the company patches nothing.
items.takeaway: Windows instances, SMB shares and Active Directory permissions: FSx for Windows File Server.
items.twin: If the stem said "The instances run Linux and access the files over NFS" instead: Amazon EFS, because it serves EC2 instances [concurrently from multiple NFS clients](../facts/efs.md#efs-concurrent-access-multiple-clients-multiple-azs).
items.say: Windows, SMB and Active Directory means FSx for Windows File Server, joined to the domain.

solvers.stem_only: Windows clients, SMB with AD permissions, shared across two AZs, least overhead: Amazon FSx for Windows File Server Multi-AZ joined to the AD domain.

items.stem: A company runs a short-lived high performance computing (HPC) simulation on Amazon EC2 Linux instances for two weeks. The input data is in an Amazon S3 bucket, and the results must be written back to the bucket. The simulation needs a file system with very high throughput. If a file server fails, the job can read the input from Amazon S3 again and repeat the failed step. Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?
keywords: the job can read the input from Amazon S3 again and repeat the failed step

options.text: Create an FSx for Lustre persistent file system linked to the bucket, and turn on daily automatic backups of the file system.
options.why: This configuration does not exist: backups are [supported only on FSx for Lustre persistent](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-lustre-backups-persistent-only-not-s3-linked-not-scratch) file systems [not linked to an Amazon S3 data repository](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-lustre-backups-persistent-only-not-s3-linked-not-scratch). Its [data is replicated](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-lustre-persistent-replicated-servers-replaced) too, which this job does not need.

options.text: Create an FSx for Lustre scratch file system linked to the bucket, and turn on daily automatic backups to protect the results.
options.why: [Backups aren’t supported on scratch file systems](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-faq-lustre-backups-not-on-scratch), so this configuration does not exist.

options.text: Create an Amazon EFS Regional file system with Provisioned throughput, and copy the input data from the bucket before the job starts.
options.why: FSx for Lustre is built for [machine learning, high-performance computing (HPC)](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-decision-guide-lustre-speed-workloads), and this option adds a full copy of the input before the job can start.
options.misconception: picks the general-purpose file system for an HPC job on S3 data

options.text: Create an FSx for Lustre scratch file system linked to the bucket, and export the results to the bucket when the job ends.
options.why: Scratch is [cost-optimized storage for short-term, processing-heavy workloads](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-lustre-use-scratch-for-short-term-persistent-for-long-term), and the link lets the job [write file system data back to S3](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-lustre-s3-presents-objects-as-files-and-writes-back).

items.explanation: The job is short-lived, and it can repeat a failed step from the data in Amazon S3. On a scratch file system the [data is not replicated](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-lustre-scratch-temporary-not-replicated), which this job accepts. The link to the bucket [transparently presents S3 objects as files](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-lustre-s3-presents-objects-as-files-and-writes-back), so the job starts without a full copy.
items.takeaway: A short HPC job that can rerun from S3: FSx for Lustre scratch, linked to the bucket.
items.twin: If the stem said "the results stay on the file system for months, and the job is sensitive to downtime" instead: a persistent file system, because it fits workloads [sensitive to disruptions in availability](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-lustre-use-scratch-for-short-term-persistent-for-long-term).

steps: I read the last sentence first: it asks for the MOST cost-effective solution.
I mark the constraints: the job is short-lived, the input is in Amazon S3, the results go back to the bucket, the job needs very high throughput, and it can repeat a failed step.
Before I look at the options, I predict an FSx for Lustre scratch file system linked to the bucket, because scratch is cost-optimized storage for short-term, processing-heavy workloads.

I remove both options with daily backups: backups are not supported on scratch file systems, and not on file systems linked to Amazon S3. I remove Amazon EFS, because FSx for Lustre is the file system built for HPC, and the EFS option copies the whole input first.
Between the persistent file system and the scratch file system, the difference is replication; the stem says the job can read its input from Amazon S3 again, so I do not pay for replicated data.
Check: the scratch file system linked to the bucket meets every constraint, and it writes the results back to the bucket. Time: 90 seconds.

solvers.stem_only: Use an FSx for Lustre scratch file system linked to the S3 bucket (data repository association): it lazy-loads input from S3, gives very high throughput, and is the cheapest Lustre type because data is not replicated; the job tolerates server loss by re-reading from S3. Write results back to S3 with an export (data repository export task or auto-export) before the file system is deleted. No backups and no persistent deployment are needed.

items.stem: A company stores about 100 GiB of application data on an Amazon EFS Regional file system that uses Bursting throughput. The file system has used all of its burst credits, and the application slows down. The application drives a steady-state, predictable throughput close to its peak all day. The company has measured this rate over several months and expects it to stay the same. The company must restore the performance of the application. Which change will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?
keywords: steady-state, predictable throughput close to its peak all day
used all of its burst credits

options.text: Switch the file system to Elastic throughput, so that throughput scales up and down with the reads and writes of the application.
options.why: Elastic works, but AWS says to use Provisioned throughput when you [know your workload's performance requirements](../facts/efs.md#efs-provisioned-use-when-known-needs-5-percent-or-more), and the company has measured its steady rate.
options.misconception: pays per use for a constant, high throughput

options.text: Switch the file system to Provisioned throughput, and set the provisioned level to the throughput that the application needs at its peak.
options.why: AWS names Provisioned throughput for [predictable and high levels of sustained throughput requirements](../facts/efs.md#efs-pricing-provisioned-throughput-predictable-sustained), and the level is [independent of the file system's size](../facts/efs.md#efs-provisioned-throughput-independent-of-size).

options.text: Keep Bursting throughput, and store extra unused data in the file system to raise the baseline throughput that the file system earns.
options.why: Bursting gives [throughput that scales with the amount of storage](../facts/efs.md#efs-bursting-scales-with-storage-size-recommended-for), so the company pays to store data that nobody reads.

options.text: Create a new file system that uses the Max I/O performance mode, and copy the application data to the new file system.
options.why: Max I/O changes the performance mode, not the throughput mode, and AWS recommends [always using General Purpose performance mode](../facts/efs.md#efs-general-purpose-always-recommended-max-io-higher-latency).

items.explanation: The load is steady, predictable and close to its peak, and the company has measured it, so it knows the throughput that it needs. With Provisioned throughput, [you specify a level of throughput](../facts/efs.md#efs-provisioned-throughput-independent-of-size) that the file system can drive, whatever its size or burst credits. Elastic throughput fits [spiky or unpredictable workloads](../facts/efs.md#efs-elastic-best-for-spiky-low-average-to-peak), which this load is not.
items.takeaway: Steady, known, high EFS throughput: Provisioned throughput at the level that the application needs.
items.twin: If the stem said "The throughput is spiky and unpredictable: the application is idle most of the day, then drives short peaks" instead: Elastic throughput, because it fits [spiky or unpredictable workloads](../facts/efs.md#efs-elastic-best-for-spiky-low-average-to-peak).

solvers.stem_only: Small data set with a steady, known throughput close to peak all day: Bursting cannot earn enough credits at 100 GiB, and Elastic suits spiky or unpredictable loads (it bills per amount of data transferred, which costs more for constant high use). The cost-effective fix is Provisioned throughput set to the known required rate.

solvers.flag: Option D is a second, weakly defensible answer: AWS itself says base throughput is proportionate to Standard storage size (50 KiBps per each GiB) and a Lambda troubleshooting page says to 'increase the size of the file system or use provisioned throughput' when burst credits run out. The stem gives no storage price, no throughput figure and no amount of extra data, so a reader cannot prove from the stem that padding with data costs more than Provisioned throughput; the saved AWS pages carry no price per GiB or per MiBps to settle it. Option C is still the AWS-recommended fix for a throughput-constrained Bursting file system with predictable sustained load, and D only works at a stated cost that the stem does not give.

items.stem: A company stores 80 TB of engineering files on one Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP volume. Engineers edit about 10% of the files every week, and those files need SSD latency. The other files are infrequently accessed. An administrator created the volume with the AWS CLI and did not set a tiering policy. The company wants to lower the storage cost without slowing down the active files. Which change will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?
keywords: created the volume with the AWS CLI and did not set a tiering policy

options.text: Change the tiering policy of the volume to All, so that all user data and snapshot data move to capacity pool storage.
options.why: All [marks all user data and snapshot data](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-ontap-tiering-policy-all-marks-everything-cold) as cold, so the files that engineers edit every week leave the SSD tier.
options.misconception: moves active data to the cold tier to save the most money

options.text: Keep the default tiering policy of the volume, because the default policy already moves cold user data to capacity pool storage.
options.why: A volume created with the AWS CLI gets Snapshot Only, which [moves only snapshot data](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-ontap-tiering-policy-snapshot-only-2-days-default-cli), so the cold user files stay on SSD storage.
options.misconception: believes that every new ONTAP volume moves cold user data to capacity pool storage

options.text: Change the tiering policy of the volume to Auto, so that cold user data and snapshots move to capacity pool storage.
options.why: Auto moves cold user data and snapshots after a cooling period that [by default is 31 days](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-ontap-tiering-policy-auto-31-days-default-console), while the active files stay on SSD.

options.text: Change the tiering policy of the volume to None, and increase the SSD storage capacity of the file system for future growth.
options.why: It works, but None [keeps all of your volume’s data](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-ontap-tiering-policy-none-keeps-all-on-ssd) on the SSD tier, so the company keeps paying SSD storage for the cold files.
options.misconception: buys more SSD storage instead of tiering the cold data

items.explanation: Most of the data is cold, and the active files need SSD latency. With the AWS CLI the default policy is Snapshot Only, which [moves only snapshot data](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-ontap-tiering-policy-snapshot-only-2-days-default-cli). The Auto policy also moves cold user data to the capacity pool tier, so the cold files stop using SSD storage, and the weekly files stay fast.
items.takeaway: On FSx for ONTAP, mostly cold data with an active part: set the tiering policy to Auto.
items.twin: If the stem said "all of the files are infrequently accessed archives" instead: the All policy, because it [marks all user data and snapshot data](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-ontap-tiering-policy-all-marks-everything-cold) as cold.

solvers.stem_only: ONTAP volume made via CLI gets the Snapshot-only tiering policy by default, so cold user data stays on SSD; set the tiering policy to Auto so cold user data and snapshots tier to the capacity pool while hot data stays on SSD.

items.stem: A company keeps application files on an Amazon EFS file system in the us-east-1 Region. The application runs on Amazon EC2 instances in that Region. The company needs cross-Region disaster recovery in us-west-2, with a recovery point objective (RPO) and a recovery time objective (RTO) of minutes. The solution must use ongoing replication. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Create an EFS replication configuration for the file system, with a new destination file system in the us-west-2 Region.
options.why: EFS replication copies the file system to the [Region or Availability Zone (AZ) of your choice](../facts/efs.md#efs-replication-destination-faq-region-or-az-of-choice), and [replication is continual](../facts/efs.md#efs-replication-rpo-rto-minutes).

options.text: Point the application in us-west-2 at the replica for writes while replication runs, so that both Regions stay active.
options.why: While replication is enabled, the replica is a [new read-only destination file system](../facts/efs.md#efs-replication-destination-read-only-while-replicating), so the writes in us-west-2 fail.

options.text: Create an AWS Backup plan that backs up the file system every day and copies each recovery point to us-west-2.
options.why: A daily backup leaves the copy in us-west-2 a day behind at worst, which misses an RPO of minutes.
options.misconception: treats daily backup copies as replication with an RPO of minutes

options.text: Run a script on an Amazon EC2 instance that copies changed files to a file system in us-west-2 every minute.
options.why: It can work, but the team runs the instance and the script, while EFS replication works [without having to manage additional infrastructure](../facts/efs.md#efs-replication-destination-faq-region-or-az-of-choice).
options.misconception: builds a custom copy job instead of the built-in replication

options.text: During a disaster, delete the replication configuration so that the replica becomes writeable, and mount the replica in us-west-2.
options.why: To fail over, you delete the replication configuration, and then [the replica becomes writeable](../facts/efs.md#efs-replication-failover-delete-configuration-replica-writeable) for the application in us-west-2.

items.explanation: EFS replication is designed to provide a recovery point objective (RPO) and a recovery time [objective (RTO) of minutes](../facts/efs.md#efs-replication-rpo-rto-minutes). In a disaster you fail over to the replica [by deleting its replication configuration](../facts/efs.md#efs-replication-failover-delete-configuration-replica-writeable), and the replica then takes the writes.
items.takeaway: EFS disaster recovery in another Region: EFS replication, then delete the configuration to fail over.
items.twin: If the stem said "read-only access for users in us-west-2" instead: the replication configuration alone, because applications can [use the replica file system in read-only mode](../facts/efs.md#efs-replication-destination-read-only-while-replicating).

solvers.stem_only: Use EFS Replication to a destination file system in us-west-2 (RPO/RTO in minutes); at failover delete the replication configuration so the read-only replica becomes writeable and point the application at it.

items.stem: A company runs a Linux application on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group. The instances share a set of files through an Amazon EFS file system. The files are production reports, and the file system must be highly available if one Availability Zone fails. The company plans to create a new file system for these files. Which file system configuration will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?
keywords: highly available if one Availability Zone fails

options.text: Create an EFS One Zone file system in one Availability Zone, and keep the automatic backups of the new file system turned on.
options.why: One Zone is [not resilient to a complete AZ outage](../facts/efs.md#efs-onezone-not-resilient-to-az-outage), and a backup restores the files later instead of keeping them available.

options.text: Create an EFS Regional file system that stores data across Availability Zones, and create a mount target in each zone.
options.why: A Regional file system gives [continuous availability to the data](../facts/efs.md#efs-regional-multi-az-continuous-availability) when one zone fails, and each zone has its own mount target.

options.text: Create an EFS Regional file system, and configure EFS Replication to a destination file system in a second AWS Region.
options.why: It works, but a Regional file system is designed to [sustain data if an AZ is lost](../facts/efs.md#efs-regional-designed-to-sustain-az-loss), so a replica in a second Region adds cost that the stem does not ask for.

options.text: Create two EFS One Zone file systems in two Availability Zones, and keep them in sync with a scheduled AWS DataSync task.
options.why: A scheduled copy runs behind the source, and someone switches the instances to the other file system after a zone fails.
options.misconception: treats a scheduled copy as high availability

items.explanation: The stem asks for files that stay available when a zone fails. A Regional file system stores data across [multiple geographically separated Availability Zones](../facts/efs.md#efs-regional-recommended-type), so the instances reach the data through the mount targets in the other zones. One Zone file systems [store data redundantly within a single AZ](../facts/efs.md#efs-faq-one-zone-single-az), so a zone outage stops access.
items.takeaway: Files that stay available through a zone failure: an EFS Regional file system, not One Zone.
items.twin: If the stem said "The files are development build artifacts that the team can re-create, and a loss of access during an Availability Zone outage is acceptable" instead: One Zone, because it suits [development, build, and staging environments](../facts/efs.md#efs-faq-one-zone-use-cases).

solvers.stem_only: Production data that must survive an AZ failure, cheapest: EFS Regional (Standard) file system with a mount target in each AZ; cross-Region replication is not required.

items.stem: A research team trains machine learning models on a 200 TB dataset that is stored in an Amazon S3 bucket. The training runs on a cluster of Linux GPU instances that needs a shared file system with very high throughput. Each training job reads only part of the dataset, and training must start as soon as possible after the cluster launches. Trained models must be stored in the bucket. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: reads only part of the dataset

options.text: Create an Amazon FSx for Lustre file system that is linked to the bucket, start training at once, and export the trained models to the bucket.
options.why: A linked file system [transparently presents S3 objects as files](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-lustre-s3-presents-objects-as-files-and-writes-back), loads content when a job first reads a file, and can [write file system data back to S3](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-lustre-s3-presents-objects-as-files-and-writes-back).

options.text: Create an Amazon FSx for Lustre file system, copy the whole dataset into it with an AWS DataSync task, and start training after the copy completes.
options.why: It works, but the bulk copy delays training and adds a task, while content is [imported automatically from S3 only when you access](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-faq-lustre-s3-object-imported-on-first-access) a linked file.

options.text: Create an Amazon EFS file system, copy the dataset into it with an AWS DataSync task, and mount the file system on every GPU instance in the cluster.
options.why: FSx for Lustre is the file system built for [machine learning, high-performance computing (HPC)](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-decision-guide-lustre-speed-workloads), and the EFS copy also delays training until it completes.

options.text: Download the part of the dataset that each job needs from the bucket to an Amazon EBS volume on every GPU instance when the instance boots.
options.why: Each instance gets a separate copy on its own volume, so the cluster has no shared file system, and every boot waits for a download.
options.misconception: separate copies on the volume of each instance work like a shared file system for a cluster

items.explanation: High throughput for machine learning and a fast start decide this question. FSx for Lustre is built for [machine learning, high-performance computing (HPC)](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-decision-guide-lustre-speed-workloads). Linked to the bucket, it [transparently presents S3 objects as files](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-lustre-s3-presents-objects-as-files-and-writes-back), and content is [imported automatically from S3 only when you access](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-faq-lustre-s3-object-imported-on-first-access) a file, so training starts without a bulk copy.
items.takeaway: FSx for Lustre linked to S3 shows the bucket as files at once and loads content on first read.
items.twin: If the stem said "Windows instances read the dataset over SMB" instead: choose FSx for Windows File Server, because AWS lists [Linux](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-compare-client-compatibility) as the client of FSx for Lustre.
items.say: Link FSx for Lustre to the bucket; jobs start at once, and data loads when a file is first read.

solvers.stem_only: Use Amazon FSx for Lustre linked to the S3 bucket. The file system imports only metadata at creation and lazy-loads file contents on first access, so training can start at once and each job pulls only the part of the dataset it reads; it gives a shared high-throughput POSIX file system for the GPU cluster. Export the trained models back to the bucket (export task or auto-export). No bulk copy with DataSync and no per-instance downloads.

items.stem: A company stores production Windows file shares on one Amazon FSx for Windows File Server file system that uses a Single-AZ deployment. Hundreds of employees map the shares over SMB every working day. The file shares must stay highly available if one Availability Zone fails, and failover must happen without manual steps. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: highly available if one Availability Zone fails

options.text: Create a Single-AZ 2 file system and move the shares to it, because a Single-AZ 2 file system fails over to another Availability Zone when its zone fails.
options.why: A Single-AZ file system has a [single Windows file server instance](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-windows-single-az-one-server-one-az-30-minutes-downtime) in one zone and [about 30 minutes of downtime](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-windows-single-az-one-server-one-az-30-minutes-downtime) during recovery, with no standby elsewhere.

options.text: Create a second Single-AZ file system in another Availability Zone, replicate the shares to it with a scheduled AWS DataSync task, and switch users after a failure.
options.why: You can use [AWS DataSync](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-faq-windows-datasync-replicate-same-and-cross-region) for periodic replication to a second file system, but users switch by hand and lose changes since the last run.
options.misconception: two file systems with a scheduled copy give the same failover as a Multi-AZ deployment

options.text: Create a Multi-AZ file system with a preferred file server and a standby file server in two Availability Zones, and move the shares to it.
options.why: A Multi-AZ file system has [a preferred AZ and a standby AZ](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-windows-multi-az-standby-two-azs-sync-replication) and gives availability by [failing over automatically to the standby AZ](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-windows-multi-az-enhanced-durability-availability-auto-failover).

options.text: Keep the Single-AZ file system, take daily backups, and restore the latest backup to a new file system in another Availability Zone after a failure.
options.why: A restore creates a new file system after the failure, so users wait for it and lose the changes made since the last backup.
options.misconception: backups that are restored after a failure make a file system highly available

items.explanation: The stem needs to survive a zone failure with automatic failover. A Multi-AZ deployment runs Windows file servers in [a preferred AZ and a standby AZ](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-windows-multi-az-standby-two-azs-sync-replication), with data [replicated synchronously within each individual AZ](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-windows-multi-az-standby-two-azs-sync-replication) and between the zones. It gives availability by [failing over automatically to the standby AZ](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-windows-multi-az-enhanced-durability-availability-auto-failover), so employees keep their shares without manual steps.
items.takeaway: For zone failures, FSx for Windows File Server needs a Multi-AZ deployment; Single-AZ has one file server in one zone.
items.twin: If the stem said "a few hours of downtime are acceptable, and cost matters most" instead: keep a Single-AZ file system with daily backups, which runs a [single Windows file server instance](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-windows-single-az-one-server-one-az-30-minutes-downtime).
items.say: Use a Multi-AZ file system: a standby file server in a second zone takes over automatically.

solvers.stem_only: Automatic AZ-level failover for FSx for Windows: move the shares to a Multi-AZ deployment (preferred and standby file servers in two AZs).

items.stem: A company wants to migrate an on-premises NetApp ONTAP storage system to AWS as a lift and shift. Linux applications use the data over NFS, and Windows users open the same volumes over SMB at the same time. The storage team already replicates volumes with NetApp SnapMirror and wants to keep its ONTAP tools. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: the same volumes over SMB at the same time

options.text: Move the Linux data to Amazon EFS and the Windows data to Amazon FSx for Windows File Server, and keep the two copies in sync with AWS DataSync.
options.why: It works, but two file systems and a sync job add overhead, while FSx for NetApp ONTAP gives [multi-protocol access](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-faq-ontap-nfs-smb-multiprotocol) to one copy of the data.

options.text: Move all data to Amazon FSx for Windows File Server, and change the Linux applications so that they read and write the files over SMB.
options.why: The Linux applications would need changes, which a lift and shift avoids, while FSx for NetApp ONTAP serves both protocols with [multi-protocol access](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-faq-ontap-nfs-smb-multiprotocol).
options.misconception: changing the Linux clients from NFS to SMB is part of a lift and shift

options.text: Move all data to Amazon FSx for OpenZFS, and serve the same volumes to the Linux applications over NFS and to the Windows users over SMB.
options.why: AWS lists [NFS 3, 4.0, 4.1, 4.2](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-compare-protocol-support) as the protocols of FSx for OpenZFS and no SMB, so the Windows users cannot open the volumes over SMB.

options.text: Migrate the volumes to Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP with NetApp SnapMirror, and serve the same volumes over NFS to Linux and over SMB to Windows.
options.why: FSx for NetApp ONTAP gives [multi-protocol access](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-faq-ontap-nfs-smb-multiprotocol) to the same data, and AWS recommends SnapMirror to [migrate your NetApp ONTAP file systems](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-ontap-snapmirror-recommended-for-migrating-onprem-netapp) to it.

items.explanation: NFS and SMB on the same volumes, a lift and shift, and SnapMirror decide this question. FSx for NetApp ONTAP supports [all versions of the Network File System (NFS)](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-faq-ontap-nfs-smb-multiprotocol) and SMB, with [multi-protocol access](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-faq-ontap-nfs-smb-multiprotocol) to the same data. AWS recommends SnapMirror to [migrate your NetApp ONTAP file systems](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-ontap-snapmirror-recommended-for-migrating-onprem-netapp), so the team keeps its tools and one copy of the data.
items.takeaway: NFS and SMB on the same data, or a NetApp source: FSx for NetApp ONTAP, migrated with SnapMirror.
items.twin: If the stem said "ZFS file servers that only Linux clients use over NFS" instead: choose [FSx for OpenZFS](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-when-to-choose-openzfs-from-zfs), which AWS recommends for ZFS servers.
items.say: FSx for ONTAP serves NFS and SMB on the same volumes, and SnapMirror moves the data.

solvers.stem_only: Lift and shift of NetApp ONTAP with multiprotocol NFS+SMB and SnapMirror tooling: Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP, migrate with SnapMirror.

items.stem: A company keeps Windows home directories on one Amazon FSx for Windows File Server file system with SSD storage. Employees map their home directories over SMB with permissions from the company's Active Directory. The data will grow to about 300 TiB within three years. Employees must keep using one share path, and the storage design must be scalable to that size. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Keep the single file system, and increase its storage capacity every quarter so that it grows in place to hold all of the home directories.
options.why: One file system holds a maximum of [64 TiB](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-windows-limit-max-storage-capacity), so it cannot grow in place to 300 TiB of home directories.

options.text: Move the home directories to one Amazon EFS file system, which grows automatically, and map it on the Windows clients as a network drive.
options.why: EFS uses the [NFS v4](../facts/efs.md#efs-faq-nfs-v4-protocol) protocol, not SMB with Active Directory permissions, so it does not serve these Windows home shares.

options.text: Create several FSx for Windows File Server file systems, and group their file shares under one Microsoft DFS Namespaces namespace that employees map as one path.
options.why: DFS Namespaces groups the shares of several file systems into [one common folder structure, or namespace](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-windows-dfs-namespaces-group-file-systems-scale-beyond-64-tib), so employees keep one path while storage grows.

options.text: Run Windows file servers on Amazon EC2 instances with Amazon EBS volumes, and group their file shares under one Microsoft DFS Namespaces namespace.
options.why: It works, but the company patches, backs up, and scales its own servers, while FSx for Windows File Server gives [fully managed Microsoft Windows file servers](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-windows-fully-managed-native-windows-file-servers-smb).

items.explanation: A single file system has a [maximum storage capacity of single file system (64 TiB)](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-windows-dfs-namespaces-group-file-systems-scale-beyond-64-tib), and the data will reach 300 TiB. DFS Namespaces groups the shares of several FSx for Windows File Server file systems into [one common folder structure, or namespace](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-windows-dfs-namespaces-group-file-systems-scale-beyond-64-tib), so employees keep one path, and every file system stays fully managed.
items.takeaway: One FSx for Windows File Server file system has a size limit; DFS Namespaces joins several under one path.
items.twin: If the stem said "the data will grow to about 40 TiB" instead: increase the storage capacity of the one file system, which holds up to [64 TiB](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-windows-limit-max-storage-capacity).
items.say: Use several FSx file systems behind one DFS namespace, because one file system has a size limit.

solvers.stem_only: One FSx for Windows file system has a maximum storage capacity well below 300 TiB, so use multiple FSx for Windows file systems grouped under one DFS Namespaces namespace for a single path.

items.stem: A company runs Linux applications on Amazon EC2 instances that share an Amazon EFS file system. The company's on-premises data center connects to the VPC through an AWS Site-to-Site VPN connection. Linux servers in the data center must now mount the same file system, but every mount attempt times out. The security group of the mount targets allows inbound traffic only from the security group of the EC2 instances. Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST secure way?
keywords: allows inbound traffic only from the security group of the EC2 instances

options.text: Add an inbound rule to the mount target security group that allows NFS traffic on TCP port 2049 from 0.0.0.0/0, and mount the file system by a mount target IP address.
options.why: It works, but every address that can reach the VPC can then try the NFS port, which is less secure than the data center's range.
options.misconception: a rule that is open to every address is acceptable because the mount targets have no public IP addresses

options.text: Attach an internet gateway to the VPC, give each mount target a public IP address, and allow TCP port 2049 from the public IP addresses of the data center.
options.why: Servers on premises mount EFS when they connect over [AWS Direct Connect or Site-to-Site VPN](../facts/efs.md#efs-onpremises-mount-via-direct-connect-or-vpn), which the company has, so internet exposure adds risk.
options.misconception: servers on premises reach EFS mount targets over the internet through public IP addresses

options.text: Add an inbound rule to the mount target security group that allows NFS traffic on TCP port 2049 from the data center's address range, and mount by a mount target IP address.
options.why: The [mount target security group](../facts/efs.md#efs-onpremises-security-group-allow-nfs-port-2049) must allow the [NFS port (2049)](../facts/efs.md#efs-onpremises-security-group-allow-nfs-port-2049) from the servers, and AWS recommends a [mount target IP address instead of](../facts/efs.md#efs-onpremises-use-mount-target-ip-instead-of-dns) a DNS name.

options.text: Add an inbound rule to the mount target security group that allows HTTPS traffic on TCP port 443 from the data center's address range, and mount by a mount target IP address.
options.why: An NFS client [can only mount a file system](../facts/efs.md#efs-nfs-client-needs-network-connection-to-port-2049) when it reaches the [NFS port (TCP port 2049)](../facts/efs.md#efs-nfs-client-needs-network-connection-to-port-2049), so a rule for HTTPS leaves the mount blocked.

items.explanation: The timeout shows a network block: an NFS client [can only mount a file system](../facts/efs.md#efs-nfs-client-needs-network-connection-to-port-2049) when it reaches the [NFS port (TCP port 2049)](../facts/efs.md#efs-nfs-client-needs-network-connection-to-port-2049) of a mount target. AWS says to [allow inbound traffic](../facts/efs.md#efs-onpremises-security-group-allow-nfs-port-2049) to the [NFS port (2049)](../facts/efs.md#efs-onpremises-security-group-allow-nfs-port-2049) from the server, and to mount by a [mount target IP address instead of](../facts/efs.md#efs-onpremises-use-mount-target-ip-instead-of-dns) a DNS name. The data center's range keeps other networks out.
items.takeaway: Servers on premises mount EFS over VPN or Direct Connect after the mount target security group allows NFS from their range.
items.twin: If the stem said "Windows servers in the data center" instead: no EFS rule helps, because an on-premises server [must have a Linux-based operating system](../facts/efs.md#efs-onpremises-server-must-be-linux); use FSx for Windows File Server.
items.say: Allow the NFS port from the data center range in the mount target security group, and mount by IP address.

solvers.stem_only: Allow inbound NFS (TCP 2049) on the mount target security group from the on-premises CIDR only, and mount by mount target IP address (EFS DNS names do not resolve on premises without extra DNS setup).

items.stem: A media company stores project files on an Amazon EFS file system that Linux editing servers mount. The files of each project are read often for about one month and then become infrequently accessed. Months later, an old project is sometimes reopened, and its files are then read many times each day by editors who need low latency. The company wants to reduce storage cost without changing the application. Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?
keywords: read many times each day by editors who need low latency

options.text: Create a lifecycle policy that moves files to EFS Infrequent Access (EFS IA) after 30 days without access and moves files back to EFS Standard on their first access.
options.why: EFS IA fits data read [a few times a quarter](../facts/efs.md#efs-faq-ia-quarter-archive-year-designed-for), and a policy can [transition files into Standard storage](../facts/efs.md#efs-lifecycle-transition-to-standard-on-first-access) on first access, so reopened projects get low latency.

options.text: Create a lifecycle policy that moves files to EFS Infrequent Access (EFS IA) after 30 days without access, because files that are read again return to EFS Standard by default.
options.why: By default, read files are [not moved back to the Standard storage class](../facts/efs.md#efs-lifecycle-default-no-move-back-to-standard), so reopened projects stay in EFS IA with [tens of milliseconds](../facts/efs.md#efs-latency-ia-archive-first-byte) of first-byte latency.

options.text: Copy files older than 30 days to an Amazon S3 bucket, and add an S3 Lifecycle rule that moves objects back to S3 Standard when an editor reads them again.
options.why: The servers read files through a mounted file system, and Amazon S3 is an [object storage service](../facts/efs.md#efs-faq-use-case-file-vs-block-vs-object), so this changes the application.

items.stem: A company is moving its Windows file shares from a file server in the company's data center to Amazon FSx for Windows File Server. Employees must keep signing in with their existing accounts, which live in the company's own Active Directory domain on domain controllers in the same data center. The data center connects to the VPC through AWS Direct Connect, and the domain controllers are reachable from the VPC. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: the domain controllers are reachable from the VPC

options.text: Create an AD Connector directory that points to the on-premises domain, and join the file system to the domain through the AD Connector directory.
options.why: [Amazon FSx does not support](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-windows-ad-connector-simple-ad-not-supported) AD Connector or Simple AD, so the file system cannot join the domain through an AD Connector directory.

options.text: Join the file system directly to the existing on-premises domain as a self-managed Active Directory, using the domain's DNS servers and a service account.
options.why: FSx for Windows File Server can join an [existing, self-managed Active Directory domain](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-windows-ad-options-aws-managed-or-self-managed) on premises, so employees keep their accounts and no new directory is created.

options.text: Create a Simple AD directory in the VPC, copy the employees' user accounts into it, and join the file system to the Simple AD domain.
options.why: [Amazon FSx does not support](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-windows-ad-connector-simple-ad-not-supported) Simple AD, and a copy of the user accounts is a second directory that the company keeps in sync.

options.text: Create an AWS Managed Microsoft AD directory with a one-way forest trust to the on-premises domain, and join the file system to the managed directory.
options.why: It works through a [one-way forest trust relationship](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-windows-resource-forest-one-way-trust), but the company then runs and pays for a second directory, which adds overhead.
options.misconception: FSx for Windows File Server has to join AWS Managed Microsoft AD, so an on-premises domain is reached through a trust

items.explanation: Employees keep their on-premises accounts, and the domain controllers are reachable over Direct Connect. An FSx for Windows File Server file system can join an [existing, self-managed Active Directory domain](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-windows-ad-options-aws-managed-or-self-managed), on premises or in the cloud, so the direct join adds no directory to run. [Amazon FSx does not support](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-windows-ad-connector-simple-ad-not-supported) AD Connector or Simple AD.
items.takeaway: FSx for Windows File Server joins AWS Managed Microsoft AD or your self-managed domain directly; AD Connector is not an option.
items.twin: If the stem said "the company has no Active Directory and wants AWS to run one" instead: create AWS Managed Microsoft AD, because you can [integrate your Amazon FSx file system](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-windows-ad-options-aws-managed-or-self-managed) with it.
items.say: Join FSx directly to the on-premises domain as a self-managed AD; FSx does not work with AD Connector.

solvers.stem_only: FSx for Windows can join a self-managed (on-premises) AD domain directly over the network connection; no AWS Directory Service needed.

items.stem: A company runs a reporting web application on Linux Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group that spans three Availability Zones behind an Application Load Balancer. The application saves each generated report as a file in a local directory. Users share report links with colleagues, and many downloads fail because the request reaches an instance that does not hold the file. Instances are added and removed during the day. The fix must need minimal code changes. What should a solutions architect do?
keywords: the request reaches an instance that does not hold the file
Instances are added and removed during the day

options.text: Turn on sticky sessions for the target group, so that the load balancer sends each user's requests to the instance that created that user's reports.
options.why: Stickiness can [bind a user's session to a specific target](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-sticky-sessions-what), but a colleague's request can reach another instance, and a removed instance takes its reports with it.

options.text: Create one Amazon EBS io2 volume with Multi-Attach turned on, and attach the volume at the report directory of every instance in the group.
options.why: Multi-Attach attaches one volume to instances [in the same Availability Zone](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-multi-attach-provisioned-iops-same-az), so it cannot serve a group that spans three zones.

options.text: Increase the deregistration delay of the target group, so that each instance finishes its open downloads before the group removes the instance.
options.why: A longer delay lets open requests finish, but each report still lives on one instance, so requests that reach other instances still fail.
options.misconception: a longer deregistration delay makes the files of one instance available to requests that reach other instances

options.text: Create an Amazon EFS file system with a mount target in each Availability Zone, and mount it at the report directory on every instance.
options.why: Instances in all three zones share one EFS file system [concurrently from multiple NFS clients](../facts/efs.md#efs-concurrent-access-multiple-clients-multiple-azs), and the application keeps writing to its directory.

items.explanation: Each report lives on one instance, and [data is not automatically copied](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-faq-data-not-copied-to-new-instances) to instances that the group launches. An EFS file system mounted at the report directory is shared [concurrently from multiple NFS clients](../facts/efs.md#efs-concurrent-access-multiple-clients-multiple-azs) in several Availability Zones, so every instance sees every report. EFS [requires no changes to your existing applications](../facts/efs.md#efs-overview-regional-linux-shared-access), because the application still writes to a directory.
items.takeaway: Files that every instance of an Auto Scaling group reads belong on a shared EFS file system, not on one instance.
items.twin: If the stem said "each user downloads only the reports that the user created, and instances are never removed" instead: sticky sessions could work, because they [bind a user's session to a specific target](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-sticky-sessions-what).
items.say: Mount one EFS file system at the report folder on every instance, so every instance sees every report.

solvers.stem_only: Make the report directory shared storage: mount an Amazon EFS file system (mount target per AZ) at that directory on every instance; no code change.

items.stem: A company is migrating an application to AWS. A PostgreSQL database runs on one Amazon EC2 instance and needs durable, low-latency block storage for a moderate, steady I/O load. Six Linux web instances in three Availability Zones must read and write the same set of uploaded files. The company does not want to copy files between instances. Which combination of actions will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way? (Select TWO.)
keywords: runs on one Amazon EC2 instance
three Availability Zones must read and write the same set of uploaded files

options.text: Store the database files on the Amazon EFS file system that the web instances also mount for the uploaded files.
options.why: The database runs on one instance, and EBS gives the [lowest-latency access to data](../facts/efs.md#efs-faq-efs-vs-ebs-vs-s3) from a single instance; the database gains nothing from sharing.

options.text: Store the database on an Amazon EBS General Purpose SSD (gp3) volume that is attached to the database instance.
options.why: Block storage is for durable, low-latency storage [attached to single Amazon EC2 instances or containers](../facts/efs.md#efs-decision-guide-block-row-single-instance), such as databases, and AWS lists gp3 for [medium sized single instance databases](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-gp3-use-cases).

options.text: Store the uploaded files on one Amazon EBS io2 volume with Multi-Attach turned on and attached to all six web instances.
options.why: Multi-Attach attaches a volume to instances [in the same Availability Zone](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-multi-attach-provisioned-iops-same-az), so one volume cannot serve web instances in three zones.

options.text: Store the database on an Amazon EBS Provisioned IOPS SSD (io2) volume with the highest IOPS level that the instance supports.
options.why: It works, but gp3 is [the lowest cost SSD volume](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-gp3-lowest-cost-ssd) type, and io2 fits loads that need [higher IOPS and throughput than gp3 volumes](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-io2-use-cases), which a moderate, steady load does not.
options.misconception: every production database needs the highest provisioned IOPS level

options.text: Store the uploaded files on one Amazon EFS file system with a mount target in each of the three Availability Zones.
options.why: File system storage gives [shared read and write access](../facts/efs.md#efs-decision-guide-file-system-row-shared-access) across instances, and one EFS file system serves clients in all three Availability Zones.

items.explanation: The database needs block storage on one instance; the uploads need one set of files that six instances share across three zones. EBS is a [block-level storage service](../facts/efs.md#efs-faq-use-case-file-vs-block-vs-object), and EFS is a [file storage service](../facts/efs.md#efs-faq-use-case-file-vs-block-vs-object) that instances use [concurrently from multiple NFS clients](../facts/efs.md#efs-concurrent-access-multiple-clients-multiple-azs).
items.takeaway: One instance with a database: EBS block storage. Many instances in several zones that share files: EFS.
items.twin: If the stem said "the database needs sustained IOPS far above what gp3 delivers" instead: choose io2 for the database, because the IOPS need then decides the volume type.
items.say: A gp3 volume for the single database instance, and one EFS file system for the shared uploads.

solvers.stem_only: Database on an EBS gp3 volume (moderate steady I/O, cheapest SSD); shared uploads on one EFS file system with a mount target in each of the three AZs.

items.stem: A company runs on-premises ZFS file servers that Linux applications access over NFS. Several times each day, test teams create writable copies of production volumes from ZFS snapshots, and scripts automate this workflow. The company wants to migrate the file servers to AWS without changing the application code or the way the teams create these copies. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: writable copies of production volumes from ZFS snapshots

options.text: Migrate the data to Amazon EFS, back up the file system with AWS Backup, and restore a recovery point to a new file system each time a team needs a copy.
options.why: It works, but each copy is a full restore with a wait and an extra file system, and AWS recommends [FSx for OpenZFS](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-when-to-choose-openzfs-from-zfs) for ZFS servers.

options.text: Migrate the data to Amazon FSx for OpenZFS, and create a writable clone volume from a point-in-time snapshot each time a team needs a copy.
options.why: FSx for OpenZFS offers [point-in-time snapshots, in-place data cloning](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-faq-openzfs-snapshots-clones-replication), and a clone is a [writable copy](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-openzfs-clone-volume-writable-instant-depends-on-snapshot) that is [created almost instantly](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-openzfs-clone-volume-writable-instant-depends-on-snapshot).

options.text: Migrate the data to Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP with NetApp SnapMirror, and create a volume from a SnapMirror copy each time a team needs a copy.
options.why: AWS recommends SnapMirror to [migrate your NetApp ONTAP file systems](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-ontap-snapmirror-recommended-for-migrating-onprem-netapp), but the source is ZFS, and the teams would change their snapshot and clone workflow.
options.misconception: NetApp SnapMirror migrates data from any file server, including ZFS servers

options.text: Migrate the data to Amazon FSx for Lustre linked to an Amazon S3 bucket, and copy a production folder to a new directory each time a team needs a copy.
options.why: FSx for Lustre is built for [machine learning, high-performance computing (HPC)](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-decision-guide-lustre-speed-workloads), and a folder copy replaces the teams' snapshot and clone workflow.
options.misconception: FSx for Lustre is the general replacement for Linux NFS file servers

items.explanation: ZFS servers and writable copies from snapshots decide this question. AWS recommends [FSx for OpenZFS](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-when-to-choose-openzfs-from-zfs) when the current storage is ZFS, and it lets you migrate [without changing your applications](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-overview-openzfs-migrate-without-changing-apps). It offers [point-in-time snapshots, in-place data cloning](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-faq-openzfs-snapshots-clones-replication), and a clone is a [writable copy](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-openzfs-clone-volume-writable-instant-depends-on-snapshot), so the teams keep their workflow.
items.takeaway: ZFS servers with snapshots and clones move to FSx for OpenZFS; NetApp systems move to FSx for NetApp ONTAP.
items.twin: If the stem said "a NetApp ONTAP system that serves NFS and SMB clients" instead: choose FSx for NetApp ONTAP, because AWS recommends SnapMirror to [migrate your NetApp ONTAP file systems](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-ontap-snapmirror-recommended-for-migrating-onprem-netapp).
items.say: FSx for OpenZFS keeps ZFS snapshots and instant writable clones, so the teams keep their workflow.

steps: I read the last sentence first: it asks for the migration with the LEAST operational overhead.
I mark the constraints: ZFS file servers, Linux clients over NFS, writable copies from snapshots several times a day, and no change to the applications or to the copy workflow.
Before I look at the options, I predict Amazon EFS, because it is the shared NFS file system for Linux clients on AWS.

I remove FSx for Lustre, because a folder copy is not a snapshot clone, and Lustre is built for machine learning and HPC. I remove FSx for NetApp ONTAP with SnapMirror, because AWS recommends SnapMirror to migrate NetApp ONTAP file systems, and these servers run ZFS.

Between Amazon EFS with AWS Backup and FSx for OpenZFS the difference is the copy workflow. My first idea breaks because each EFS copy becomes a full restore, while FSx for OpenZFS offers point-in-time snapshots and in-place data cloning, and AWS recommends it for ZFS servers.
Check: FSx for OpenZFS keeps NFS for the applications, and a clone is a writable copy created almost instantly from a snapshot. Time: 90 seconds.

solvers.stem_only: Migrate to Amazon FSx for OpenZFS: it is a managed ZFS file system accessed over NFS, so Linux applications need no code change, and it supports point-in-time snapshots and writable clone volumes created from a snapshot, which keeps the test teams' snapshot-to-clone workflow (automated through the FSx API or CLI).
